questions.question: What are the two main stream types in Java I/O and when do you use each?
questions.title: Byte Streams vs Character Streams
questions.direct_answer: Java I/O has two stream families: byte streams (InputStream/OutputStream) for binary data like images and files, and character streams (Reader/Writer) for text data. Character streams handle character encoding automatically; byte streams work with raw bytes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java I/O fundamentals and when to choose each stream type
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using byte streams for text files and manually handling encoding
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that InputStreamReader bridges byte streams to character streams with encoding

sections.title: Two Stream Families for Different Data
sections.content:
A **stream** in Java is simply a flow of data you read or write one piece at a time, like water through a pipe. Java splits streams into two families because text and binary data are not the same thing.

**Byte streams** move raw 8-bit bytes. Their base classes are `InputStream` and `OutputStream`. Use them for binary files — images, PDFs, audio — where every byte must arrive untouched.

**Character streams** move text. Their base classes are `Reader` and `Writer`, and they convert bytes to characters using a **charset** like UTF-8. One letter such as é may be several bytes, and the character stream does that math for you.

How do they connect? The bridge classes `InputStreamReader` and `OutputStreamWriter` turn bytes into characters with a charset you pick.

- **Byte stream** handles binary with no decoding
- **Character stream** handles text with automatic decoding

> **The gotcha:** reading a UTF-8 file with a byte stream and calling `new String(bytes)` only guesses the encoding — and it breaks on the first accented character.

sections.title: Byte Streams vs Character Streams
sections.content:
amber|Byte streams|~InputStream / OutputStream|raw 8-bit bytes|binary-safe|images, audio, PDFs
blue|Character streams|~Reader / Writer|chars plus charset|text-safe|.txt, .csv, .json
emerald|The bridge|~InputStreamReader|OutputStreamWriter|bytes to chars|always set UTF-8

sections.title: Pick the Family from the Data
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB D["Data to move"] --> Q{"Binary or text?"} Q -- Binary --> B["Byte stream
InputStream / OutputStream"] Q -- Text --> C["Character stream
Reader / Writer"] B --> R["Raw bytes, no decoding"] C --> E["Charset decodes bytes to chars"] ``` The first question is always whether the data is binary or text — that single choice picks the stream family.

sections.title: Byte Stream for Binary, Character Stream for Text
Byte Streams vs Character Streams
sections.content:
| Aspect | Byte Streams | Character Streams |
|---|---|---|
| Base Classes | InputStream, OutputStream | Reader, Writer |
| Unit of Data | 8-bit bytes | 16-bit Unicode characters |
| Encoding Handling | Manual — you decode bytes | Automatic with charset |
| Use Cases | Images, videos, binary files | Text files, logs, JSON, XML |
| Example Classes | FileInputStream, ByteArrayOutputStream | FileReader, BufferedWriter |

sections.title: When to Use Each Stream Type
sections.content:
Use **byte streams** when copying files without caring about content (a backup utility), reading image bytes to send over HTTP, or working with binary protocols like reading Java class files.

Use **character streams** when reading an application.properties file, writing application logs, parsing CSV data, or reading user-uploaded text where encoding matters. In a Spring Boot app you would use a BufferedReader with UTF-8 to read a JSON config file, but a FileInputStream to read a keystore file for SSL certificates. The encoding matters for text — a Chinese character might be one byte in GB2312 or three bytes in UTF-8.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using FileInputStream for text files**: Freshers often read a log or config file with FileInputStream, then convert bytes to a String with new String(bytes). This fails when the file uses UTF-8 with special characters — use FileReader or Files.readString() instead.
- **Not specifying charset**: Using FileReader() without StandardCharsets.UTF_8 makes your code platform-dependent — it works on a Linux dev machine but breaks on a Windows server with a different default encoding.
- **Mixing stream types**: Trying to wrap an OutputStream with a Reader, which will not compile — use InputStreamReader as the bridge between byte and character streams.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Byte streams**: use InputStream/OutputStream for binary data like images, PDFs, or raw file copying where encoding doesn't matter
- **Character streams**: use Reader/Writer for text data where character encoding (UTF-8, ISO-8859-1) must be handled correctly
- **Encoding matters**: a character like é or 中 needs multiple bytes in UTF-8 — character streams handle this translation automatically
- **InputStreamReader bridge**: converts an InputStream to a Reader with a specified charset, letting you read bytes as characters with proper encoding
- **Default encoding trap**: FileReader() uses the platform default encoding — always specify StandardCharsets.UTF_8 explicitly in production code
- **Modern alternative**: Files.readString(path, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) and Files.readAllBytes(path) from java.nio.file are simpler for most file operations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Java I/O has **two main families**: byte streams and character streams. Byte streams, with `InputStream` and `OutputStream` as the base classes, work with raw bytes — you'd use them for binary data like images, PDFs, or video files. Character streams, with `Reader` and `Writer`, work with text and automatically handle character encoding.

So if you're reading a JSON config file or writing application logs, you want character streams because they understand that one character might need multiple bytes in UTF-8. The key difference is simple: byte streams just move bytes around, but character streams translate between bytes and characters using a charset.

One mistake freshers make is using `FileInputStream` to read text files, then manually building a String from the bytes. That's error-prone because you might get the encoding wrong. Just use `FileReader` with `StandardCharsets.UTF_8`, or better yet, the modern `Files.readString` method. And if you need to bridge the two, `InputStreamReader` wraps an InputStream and gives you a Reader with a specified encoding.

questions.question: What is the Java I/O stream class hierarchy?
questions.title: Java I/O Class Hierarchy
questions.direct_answer: Java I/O has four abstract base classes: InputStream and OutputStream for byte streams, Reader and Writer for character streams. Concrete classes like FileInputStream, BufferedReader, and FileWriter extend these. The hierarchy uses the Decorator pattern to wrap streams and add functionality like buffering.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the fundamental I/O class structure and how stream wrapping works through the Decorator pattern
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not recognizing that BufferedReader wraps another Reader, or trying to use byte and character streams interchangeably
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explicitly mention the Decorator pattern and explain why Java separates byte and character streams (encoding handling)

sections.title: Four Roots and the Decorator Pattern
sections.content:
The Java I/O classes are organized as a small family tree with four roots. Two roots, `InputStream` and `OutputStream`, handle bytes. The other two, `Reader` and `Writer`, handle characters. Every concrete class you use extends one of these four.

Why a tree? It lets Java share one set of method names across many sources — a file, an array, a network socket — so `read()` means the same thing everywhere.

How do the classes combine? Through the **Decorator pattern**: you wrap one stream in another to add a feature. A common text-reading stack is `BufferedReader` wrapping `InputStreamReader` wrapping `FileInputStream`. The file class talks to the disk, the reader decodes bytes to characters, and the buffer adds fast line-by-line reads.

- **Concrete classes** give you the data source
- **Decorator classes** add buffering, encoding, or typed reads

> **The gotcha:** wrapping order matters — `new BufferedReader(new FileInputStream(...))` will not compile, because a BufferedReader needs a Reader, not a raw byte stream.

sections.title: The java.io Stream Hierarchy
sections.content:
amber|InputStream (abstract)|~FileInputStream|BufferedInputStream|ByteArrayInputStream|read() bytes
blue|OutputStream (abstract)|~FileOutputStream|BufferedOutputStream|ByteArrayOutputStream|write() bytes
emerald|Reader / Writer|~FileReader / FileWriter|BufferedReader / BufferedWriter|InputStreamReader bridge|char-based

sections.title: A Typical Wrapping Chain
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB F["FileInputStream
reads raw bytes"] --> I["InputStreamReader
decodes with charset"] I --> B["BufferedReader
adds readLine"] B --> L["Your code
reads lines"] ``` Each layer adds exactly one job, and closing the outer BufferedReader closes the whole chain.

sections.title: Stream Hierarchy and Wrapping in Action
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not understanding wrapping order**: Freshers try new BufferedReader(new FileInputStream(...)) which will not compile because BufferedReader expects a Reader, not an InputStream — you need InputStreamReader in between.
- **Forgetting to close all layers**: Closing only the outermost stream is correct (it closes the inner ones), but freshers sometimes try to close each layer individually, which can cause exceptions.
- **Using FileReader without charset**: FileReader() uses the platform default encoding — windows-1252 on Windows, UTF-8 on Linux — making behavior unpredictable across environments. Always use InputStreamReader with explicit StandardCharsets.UTF_8.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Four base classes**: InputStream and OutputStream for bytes, Reader and Writer for characters — all concrete I/O classes extend these
- **Decorator pattern**: streams wrap other streams to add functionality (buffering, encoding, type conversion) without modifying the original
- **Typical wrapping chain**: BufferedReader wraps InputStreamReader wraps FileInputStream, where each layer adds a capability
- **Bridge classes**: InputStreamReader and OutputStreamWriter convert between byte streams and character streams with a specified charset
- **Buffering is critical**: BufferedReader/BufferedWriter add an 8KB buffer, reducing disk I/O from thousands of operations to dozens for typical files
- **Close outer stream only**: try-with-resources on the outermost stream automatically closes all wrapped inner streams in reverse order
- **Modern alternative**: java.nio.file.Files methods like readString(), newBufferedReader(), and copy() handle the wrapping internally

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The Java I/O class hierarchy has **four abstract base classes** at the top. For byte streams, you have `InputStream` and `OutputStream`. For character streams, you have `Reader` and `Writer`. Every concrete I/O class extends one of these four.

The clever part is how Java uses the **Decorator pattern** for composition. You wrap one stream inside another to add functionality. To read a text file efficiently, you'd wrap a `FileInputStream` in an `InputStreamReader` to handle encoding, then wrap that in a `BufferedReader` to add buffering and line-by-line reading. Each layer adds one capability.

A common mistake is trying to wrap a `BufferedReader` directly around a `FileInputStream`. That won't compile, because BufferedReader expects a Reader, not an InputStream — you need InputStreamReader as the bridge. In modern Java, the `Files` class handles all this wrapping internally, so `Files.readString` is much simpler for most use cases.

questions.question: What are the key read() and write() method signatures in Java I/O?
questions.title: Java I/O Read and Write Methods
questions.direct_answer: InputStream.read() returns one byte as an int (0-255) or -1 when the stream ends. BufferedReader.readLine() returns a String per line or null at end. OutputStream.write(int b) writes one byte. Reading one byte at a time with read() is extremely inefficient — always use read(byte[]) to read chunks or use buffered streams.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of the core I/O API signatures and understanding of performance implications in different read/write patterns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using read() in a tight loop without buffering, causing thousands of disk I/O operations instead of batching reads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why read() returns int instead of byte (to distinguish -1 end-of-stream from byte value 255) and demonstrate byte array bulk reading

sections.title: Core Read and Write Signatures
sections.content:
At the lowest level, reading in Java means calling `read()` to pull one piece of data, and writing means calling `write()` to push one out. For byte streams, `read()` returns an `int` from 0 to 255 for the next byte, or -1 when the stream ends.

Why an int and not a byte? Java's `byte` is signed (-128 to 127), so it can't tell the value 255 apart from a special end marker. Using `int` leaves room for the -1 sentinel.

Reading one byte per call is correct but slow — a 1 MB file becomes a million system calls. The bulk overload `read(byte[] buf)` fills an array and returns how many bytes it actually read, turning a million calls into a few hundred. For text, `BufferedReader.readLine()` returns a whole line, or `null` at the end.

- **read()** returns one byte as an int, or -1 at the end
- **read(byte[])** returns a chunk and the count actually read
- **readLine()** returns one line of text, or null at the end

> **The gotcha:** `read(byte[])` may fill the array only partway, so you must write the first count bytes, never the whole buffer.

sections.title: read() and write() Signatures
sections.content:
amber|read()|~int: one byte (0-255)|-1 at end of stream|blocks until data|cast to byte
blue|read(byte[] b)|~fills the array|returns the count read|-1 at EOF|loop until -1
emerald|write|~write(int) one byte|write(byte[], off, len)|flush to commit|Reader / Writer mirror these

sections.title: The Bulk Read-Write Loop
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB S["read(byte[] buf)"] --> C{"Returned -1?"} C -- No --> W["write(buf, 0, count)"] W --> S C -- Yes --> E["End of stream
stop the loop"] ``` The loop keeps reading chunks and writing exactly what it read until the count comes back as -1.

sections.title: Read and Write Method Usage Patterns
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reading single bytes in a loop**: Using while((b = input.read()) != -1) for large files causes catastrophic performance — every read() is a system call. Always read into a byte array buffer instead.
- **Ignoring read() return value**: Assuming read(byte[]) always fills the entire array — it returns the count actually read (may be less than buffer.length at the end), so you must write only that many bytes.
- **Casting int to byte incorrectly**: Doing (byte)input.read() loses the -1 end-of-stream marker because -1 as a byte equals 255 — keep the int and check for -1 before casting.
- **Not using BufferedReader for text**: Reading text with a raw FileInputStream and handling lines by hand instead of using BufferedReader.readLine(), which does it correctly.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **read() returns int**: InputStream.read() returns 0-255 for a byte value or -1 for end-of-stream — int, not byte, so -1 is distinct from value 255
- **Bulk read performance**: read(byte[] buffer) is far faster than read() in a loop because it batches disk I/O — always prefer bulk reads
- **read() return value is critical**: read(byte[]) returns the count of bytes actually read (may be less than buffer.length) — write only that many bytes
- **readLine() returns null**: BufferedReader.readLine() returns a String per line or null at end — null is your loop terminator, not an empty string
- **write(int b) low 8 bits**: OutputStream.write(int) only writes the low 8 bits — write(257) writes one byte with value 1
- **Buffer size matters**: a typical buffer is 4KB-8KB — too small wastes system calls, too large wastes memory for little gain
- **Modern convenience methods**: Files.readAllBytes() and Files.readAllLines() handle buffering and closing automatically for files that fit in memory

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The core read and write methods have signatures you need to know cold. `InputStream.read()` with no arguments returns an **int** — not a byte — with values zero to 255 for the next byte, or **negative one** when the stream ends. It returns int instead of byte because Java's byte type is signed, so it can't hold both the value 255 and a distinct end-of-stream marker.

Reading one byte at a time is extremely inefficient. A one-megabyte file read byte by byte is a million system calls. Instead, use `read(byte[] buf)`, which fills the buffer and returns the count actually read. That count might be less than the buffer size at the end, so you must use the return value when writing.

For text, `BufferedReader.readLine()` returns a String per line, or `null` when the file ends. A common mistake freshers make is reading single bytes in a tight loop. Always read in chunks with a byte array, and never ignore the count returned by read.

familiarity_anchors: turning pages until the book ends
scooping water by the bucket, not the drop
a cashier scanning items until none remain
speakable_v2.hook: When a read call returns negative one, that's not an error. It's how a Java stream says it has nothing left to give.

beats.text: The core methods are small. read pulls the next byte as an int from zero to 255. write pushes one byte out. readLine on a BufferedReader hands back a whole line of text.
read returns an int so it can signal the end. A Java byte is signed, so it can't reserve a spare value. Negative one becomes the clean end-of-stream marker.

items: read with no arguments returns one byte, or negative one at the end.
read with a byte array fills a buffer and returns the count read.
readLine returns a full line of text, or null when the file is done.

beats.text: Picture copying a file. You read into an eight-kilobyte buffer and write back exactly the count you got. Here's the non-obvious part. The last chunk often fills the buffer only partway. Writing the whole array would then append leftover garbage.

items: Reading one byte at a time in a loop, which crawls on large files.
Ignoring the count from read and writing the entire buffer every time.

speakable_v2.cap: So read and write look simple, but the return values carry the real rules. Honor negative one and the byte count, and your loops stay correct.

questions.question: Why is it critical to close streams in Java and what happens if you don't?
questions.title: Closing Java Streams
questions.direct_answer: Streams hold operating system resources like file descriptors and network sockets. If you don't close them, these resources leak and eventually exhaust the OS limit, causing 'Too many open files' errors that crash your application. Always use try-with-resources to guarantee closure even when exceptions occur.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of resource management and production reliability — critical for writing code that doesn't leak resources under load
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Closing streams only in the happy path or in a finally block without null checks, missing the resource leak when exceptions happen
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show try-with-resources syntax and explain that it handles close() even during exceptions, replacing manual finally blocks

sections.title: OS Resources and the Leak Danger
sections.content:
Closing a stream means telling the operating system you're done with the file or socket it opened for you. When you open a stream, the OS hands the JVM a **file descriptor** — a small numbered ticket that tracks the open resource.

Why it matters: every process gets a limited number of these tickets, often 1024 on Linux. If you open streams without closing them, the tickets leak. Garbage collection doesn't help — collecting the `FileInputStream` object does not return its descriptor.

Eventually the process runs out, and the next open throws **Too many open files**, crashing the app. Closing also flushes buffered writes, so an unclosed writer can silently lose data.

The fix is **try-with-resources**: declare the stream in the `try(...)` header and Java calls `close()` for you, even when the body throws.

- **Open a stream** and a descriptor is borrowed
- **Forget to close** and that descriptor leaks
- **try-with-resources** makes the close guaranteed

> **The gotcha:** a `close()` at the end of a plain try body is skipped whenever an exception fires first — only try-with-resources is leak-proof.

sections.title: Why You Must Close Streams
sections.content:
amber|Why close|~frees OS file descriptors|flushes buffered writes|releases file locks|prevents leaks
blue|If you don't|~too many open files|lost buffered data|locked files on Windows|resource exhaustion
emerald|How|~try-with-resources|auto-closes in reverse|no manual finally|closes even on exception

sections.title: The Life of a File Descriptor
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB O["open() a stream"] --> D["OS lends a file descriptor"] D --> Q{"Closed properly?"} Q -- Yes --> R["Descriptor returned"] Q -- No --> L["Descriptor leaks"] L --> X["Too many open files
app crashes"] ``` Every borrowed descriptor must come back, and try-with-resources guarantees the return trip.

sections.title: No try-with-resources: leak on exception
try-with-resources: always closed
Proper Closure with Multiple Resources
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Closing only in the happy path**: Writing reader.close() at the end of the try block, which never runs if an exception occurs during reading — the resource leaks. Use try-with-resources instead.
- **Null checks in finally**: Writing a finally block with if (reader != null) reader.close() — verbose, error-prone (close can throw IOException), and unnecessary when try-with-resources exists.
- **Not understanding scope**: Declaring the resource outside the try block so it can't go in the try header — declare it in the try parentheses instead.
- **Ignoring wrapper resources**: Closing only the FileInputStream but not the BufferedReader that wraps it — close the outermost wrapper, which closes inner streams automatically.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **File descriptors are limited**: operating systems cap open files per process (often 1024-4096) — exceeding it crashes your app with Too many open files
- **Garbage collection doesn't close**: even when your stream object is collected, the OS file descriptor stays open until close() is explicitly called
- **try-with-resources syntax**: try (var resource = ...) { } automatically calls close() when the block exits, even on exception
- **AutoCloseable interface**: any class implementing AutoCloseable (streams, readers, JDBC objects, HTTP clients) works in try-with-resources
- **Multiple resources**: try (var r1 = ...; var r2 = ...) closes them in reverse order (r2 then r1)
- **Production failure pattern**: resource leaks are silent in development but catastrophic under load — one leak per request crashes a busy service
- **Close outer wrapper only**: when streams are wrapped, closing the outermost closes the inner streams automatically

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Closing streams is **critical** because they hold operating system resources. When you open a file in Java, the JVM asks the OS for a **file descriptor** — the OS-level handle for the open file. Every process has a limit, typically one thousand to four thousand descriptors. If you don't close your streams, you leak these descriptors. They stay allocated even after the garbage collector reclaims your stream object. Eventually you hit the limit and get a `Too many open files` error, which crashes the app.

The solution is **try-with-resources**. You declare your resource in the try parentheses, like `try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(...))`, then your code block. When the block exits — normally or through an exception — Java automatically calls close. It handles all the edge cases: exceptions during close, and multiple resources closed in reverse order.

The key insight for freshers is that this isn't just good practice — it's mandatory for production reliability. Resource leaks are silent killers. Your code works fine in testing with ten requests, but fails under real load.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 service that opens config files and log files per request
familiarity_anchors: borrowing a tool and giving it back
speakable_v2.hook: Every open stream borrows a file descriptor from the OS. Leak enough of them and your app dies with too many open files.

beats.text: Closing a stream returns the operating system resource it holds. Open a file and the OS lends the JVM a file descriptor. Close the stream and that descriptor goes back.
Each process gets a limited pool of descriptors. Without closing, they leak one by one. The garbage collector won't save you, because it doesn't free descriptors on a schedule you control.

items: Close in the happy path only, and any exception skips it.
Close in a finally block, which always runs but reads as clunky.
Use try-with-resources, and Java closes the stream even when the body throws.

beats.text: Picture a service that reads a config file on every request. Here's the non-obvious part. One leaked descriptor per request looks fine in testing, then crashes the service within hours under real traffic.

items: Putting close at the end of the try body, so an exception leaks the stream.
Closing each wrapped layer by hand instead of just the outer one.

speakable_v2.cap: So a stream isn't really yours; it's borrowed from the OS. Try-with-resources hands it back every single time.

questions.question: What is the difference between java.io and java.nio in Java?
questions.title: java.io vs java.nio
questions.direct_answer: java.io is stream-based and blocking — threads wait for I/O completion. java.nio (New I/O) is buffer and channel-based with non-blocking I/O support. For most Java backend work, java.nio.file (Path, Files) is preferred for file operations; java.nio channels for high-performance network I/O.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Java I/O evolution and when to use modern APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking java.nio is only for network programming — java.nio.file is better for file ops too
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Files.readAllBytes(), Files.readString(), Files.copy() as modern alternatives

sections.title: From Blocking Streams to Flexible Channels
sections.content:
Both `java.io` and `java.nio` move data in and out of your program — they're just two generations of the same idea. `java.io` came first, in 1996, built around **streams** that read data in order, one chunk at a time. Its calls are **blocking**: when you call `read()`, the thread stops and waits until data arrives.

`java.nio` (New I/O) arrived in 2002 with **buffers** and **channels**. A channel can read and write, and a single thread can watch many channels at once instead of blocking on each — that's **non-blocking** I/O.

The part beginners miss: the slice you'll actually use most is `java.nio.file`, added in Java 7. Its `Path` and `Files` classes replace the clunky old `File` class.

- **java.io** gives you simple blocking streams
- **java.nio channels** give you scalable non-blocking sockets
- **java.nio.file** gives you the modern file API (`Files`, `Path`)

> **The gotcha:** nio sounds like it's only for networking, but `java.nio.file` is the everyday way to read and write files today.

sections.title: java.io vs java.nio

amber|java.io|~stream-oriented|blocking|simple read / write loops|one thread per stream

sections.title: Which API Should You Reach For?
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB N["What do you need?"] -->|File work| F["java.nio.file
Files, Path"] N -->|Thousands of sockets| C["java.nio channels
non-blocking"] N -->|Legacy or stream API| IO["java.io streams"] ``` For everyday backend work the answer is almost always java.nio.file.

sections.title: Same Task in java.io and NIO.2 Files
java.io vs java.nio
sections.content:
| Aspect | java.io | java.nio |
|---|---|---|
| Core Abstraction | Streams (sequential flow) | Buffers + Channels (random access) |
| I/O Model | Blocking — thread waits | Non-blocking option available |
| Direction | Unidirectional (in or out) | Bidirectional (read and write) |
| File Operations | File class with limited API | Path and Files with rich API |
| Performance | Unbuffered by default | Buffer-based, often faster |

sections.title: When to Use Each API
sections.content:
Use **java.nio.file** for all file operations in modern Java backends — Files.readString(), Files.copy(), and Files.walk() are cleaner and handle symbolic links, permissions, and atomic operations that java.io.File can't.

Use **java.nio channels** (SocketChannel, FileChannel) when building high-performance network servers where one thread must handle thousands of concurrent connections — think chat servers or WebSocket backends.

Use **java.io** only when maintaining legacy code or working with APIs that expect an InputStream or OutputStream, like a Servlet's request.getInputStream(). For typical Spring Boot apps reading config files or writing logs, java.nio.file is the clear winner.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking java.nio is only for networking**: Freshers hear non-blocking I/O and assume it's only for network programming, missing that java.nio.file is the modern way to work with files — better than java.io.File for everyday tasks.
- **Using File instead of Path**: Still using new File() and file.exists() instead of Path.of() and Files.exists(), missing atomic file moves, proper symbolic-link handling, and better exception messages.
- **Ignoring charset in Files methods**: Calling Files.readAllLines(path) without the charset parameter uses the platform default encoding — always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8 as the second argument.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **java.io model**: stream-based, blocking I/O where threads wait for operations to complete — simple but limited scalability
- **java.nio model**: buffer and channel-based with optional non-blocking I/O, letting one thread manage multiple connections efficiently
- **java.nio.file advantage**: Path and Files are modern replacements for File, with better error handling, atomic operations, and symbolic-link support
- **Blocking vs non-blocking**: java.io always blocks the calling thread, java.nio can check channel readiness with a Selector without blocking on each channel
- **Common Files operations**: Files.readString(), Files.readAllBytes(), Files.copy(), and Files.move() are one-line replacements for verbose java.io code
- **When java.nio shines**: high-concurrency network servers benefit from non-blocking channels and a Selector
- **Default choice**: use java.nio.file for file operations in all new code — use java.io streams only when an API requires InputStream/OutputStream

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
`java.io` and `java.nio` are two different I/O models. **java.io** is the original API from the nineties, built around streams that are blocking. When you call read on an InputStream, your thread stops and waits until data arrives. It's simple but limited.

**java.nio**, or New I/O, was added in 2002 with a buffer and channel model. Channels are bidirectional, and the big advantage is non-blocking I/O — a single thread can manage thousands of connections by checking which channels are ready, instead of blocking on each one.

But here's what freshers miss: the most useful part of java.nio for typical backend work is `java.nio.file`, added in Java 7. The `Path` and `Files` classes are far better than the old `File` class. `Files.readString` reads a whole file in one line with proper charset handling, and `Files.copy` does atomic file copying. For everyday Spring Boot work, java.nio.file is the clear winner; you'd reach for java.nio channels mainly when handling thousands of concurrent sockets.

groups.heading: java.io
groups.text: The original API from the nineties. It's stream-based and blocking. A read call waits until the data shows up.

groups.heading: java.nio
groups.text: The newer API with buffers and channels. It can run non-blocking. It also adds java.nio.file, with the modern Path and Files helpers.

items: Reach for java.nio.file for nearly all file work.
Reach for java.nio channels when one thread must handle thousands of live sockets.
Stick with java.io only for legacy code or APIs that demand an InputStream.

beats.text: Here's the trap. People hear nio and picture network sockets only. But Files.readString and Files.copy live in java.nio.file. They're the cleanest way to touch a file today.

speakable_v2.cap: So java.io is the classic stream API, and java.nio is the scalable one. For files, java.nio.file wins almost every time.
